title: Ag'waneq
audio_transcript:
The model you see is a recreation of the Village of Afognak.  
On March 27, 1964, the 9.2 magnitude Good Friday Earthquake and resulting tsunamis destroyed much of Afognak village. Saltwater inundation contaminated wells, structures were swept away, and the site was deemed uninhabitable. 
With federal assistance and support from the International Lions Club, survivors were relocated to a newly constructed community on Kodiak Island, named Port Lions. Others moved to Kodiak, Anchorage, or the lower 48. Afognak Island itself has remained uninhabited since 1964, though it is not abandoned culturally or spiritually. 
In 1971, the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) formally recognized the Native Village of Afognak as a federally recognized tribe and led to the creation of Afognak Native Corporation. 
If you listened to the audio guide in order, you should have a basic understanding of all the hardships our ancestors endured.  I also want to assure you we are still here today.  The success of the Afognak Native Corporation and the Afognak people isn’t by chance.  It is a direct correlation between our ancestors’ ability to persevere and adapt to any challenge that was handed to them.

title: Amerikaansat uksuat
audio_transcript:
When the United States purchased Alaska on March 30, 1867, for $7.2 million, the treaty ignored the existence of Alaska Native land ownership and sovereignty.   Alaska Native peoples—including Alutiiq/Sugpiaq, were neither parties to the treaty nor recognized as landholders. The treaty referred vaguely to Native peoples as “uncivilized tribes,” leaving  legal status of Alaska Natives unresolved under U.S. law.
For Rural communities, the transfer of power did not end colonial control—it changed its form.
Under Russian rule, Native people were exploited through forced labor and hostage-taking, but villages, subsistence cycles, and land use were largely acknowledged in practice.
Under U.S. rule, settlers, companies, and the federal government asserted ownership of land outright, leading to dispossession at a much larger scale.
The key shift was, Russians controlled people.  Americans claimed the land.
Native land use—seasonal camps, hunting grounds, fishing sites, sacred places—did not fit American property law, which required fenced, surveyed, and “improved” land. As a result, Native villages were often labeled “squatters” on their own land.
After the sale, the U.S. implemented assimilation programs like those used elsewhere.
Mission and government schools punished Native languages and culture.  Children were removed from families or sent to boarding schools
Religion and Culture
•	Traditional spiritual practices were discouraged or outlawed
•	English replaced Native languages in public life
Governance
•	Traditional leadership systems were ignored by U.S. authorities
These policies caused language loss, cultural disruption, and intergenerational trauma that communities continue to address today. 

For many Alaska Native communities, 1867 marks not a transfer of land, but the beginning of a new era of struggle—one whose effects are still visible in land ownership, language revitalization, health, and governance today.

title: Exhibit 11
audio_transcript:
Russian traders would take the women and children hostage.  They threatened to kill them if the men didn’t bring them furs.  In this tour we talked about when we hunt. If you didn’t fish for salmon when they returned you wouldn’t have fish for the winter.  Men had to hunt for the sea otter to protect their families.  Alutiiq people didn’t eat sea otter.  The people didn’t have enough food for the winter and starved.  
Russians didn’t come to Alaska looking to acculturate Alaska Natives.  They came here to make money.  They needed Native men to hunt and trade. If it’s fishing season, you fish.  If it’s berry picking time, you pick berries.  When this is done you hunt for animals you could use their fur to keep you warm during the winter.  The Russians wanted Native men to hunt for fur animals more often so they could make more money.
The Russian Orthodox church did advocate for the Alutiiq people.  Before they arrived, the people were treated as less than humans.  The Russian Orthodox faith is still practice by many Alutiiq people.  Today the services are conducted in the English language.  Up until recently it was still done in the Russian language.  Late Fr. Michael Oleksa saw the church was losing young Native people.  Grandparents and parents spoke Russian.  Their children and grandchildren went to American public schools and where punished if they didn’t speak on English.  When they attended church, they didn’t understand what was happening or what they were hearing.  As a result, the number of attendees has declined over the years.

title: Exhibit 10
audio_transcript:
Trade among Kodiak tribes was more than a barter. It was a cultural practice that reinforced alliances, shared knowledge, and maintained social ties. The exchange of goods also facilitated the spread of tools, art styles, and ceremonial practices. Because Kodiak’s location made it a hub for marine resources, it often acted as a middleman in larger Alaskan trade networks, connecting inland and coastal communities.
Archaeological and ethnographic evidence shows that Kodiak tribes were part of regional and interregional trade systems. These networks linked Kodiak to other coastal Alaskan groups, the Bering Sea, and the Aleutian Islands. Walrus ivory and Southeast Alaska dentalium shells can be found on Afognak and Kodiak Islands.  Items like whale oil and baleen could be traded with Yup’ik and Unangan communities, while feathers and shells from the Inupiaq and St. Lawrence Island Yupik were exchanged for fish and plant foods.
Wars did break out amongst tribes.  When it did Alutiiq Warriors had developed tactics to defend the Island. Warriors went into battle wearing helmets, chest plates, and carried shields.  Russian sailors described the warriors wearing various hats, many fantastical ones, made from wood or thick animal skins.  There was also mention of a collar made of tightly woven sinew that protected the neck.   To intimidate the enemy, warriors would paint their faces red and shout fierce battle cries.  
Body armor was worn by every warrior.  Most are described as made with slates of wood, although there are stories of armor fashioned with whale bones.  When attacking warriors used shields to create a phalanx.  When the warriors advanced, even musket balls could not penetrate their defenses.

title: Iqallusuwakamta
description: A variety of fish are the most important foods in the Alutiiq world. as they can be caught in quantity, dried, and stored for later use.
audio_transcript:
I remember my grandmother telling me one time, “I’m going to teach you about “uncommon sense”.  I said grandma, it’s called common sense.  She said, “There is nothing common about sense.”   Our grandparents grew up in a time before Alaska was a state.  At that time there were no regulations.  People looking to get rich in Alaska came in droves to find their fortune.  Commercial fishing companies from Seattle would completely cover the mouth of salmon spawning river catching all the fish. Yes, - they – did get rich.  In the western definition they became monetarily rich.  My grandmother would say, those people have no common sense.
In early spring elders will go collect migratory bird eggs.  They would take all the eggs because the birds would lay another clutch.  The second time elders would go bird egg collecting they’d teach the youth to only take one and leave the rest…. ensuring the birds would continue to come back every year.  This thought was traditionally applied to salmon as well.  If you catch all the salmon, there will be none for future generations.
Fishing is still an important part of Alutiiq life.  It’s become increasingly challenging to make a living and provide food for the village.  The trollers in the Berring Sea are like the nets covering the mouth of the river.  Catching everything and leaving nothing for future generations.

title: Pisuwakamta
audio_transcript:
The seasons and the migration patterns of the animals dictated when hunting would take place.  Compared to other regions, Southcentral Alaska had a longer window of opportunity.  The ocean surrounding Kodiak and Afognak stayed liquid all year round.  Kayaks could be launched from the beaches in front of the villages.  On the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, Yup’ik and Cup’ik hunters might have to use dog teams to tow their kayaks 40 miles out to the edge of the pack ice.  
This exhibit mentions waterproof clothing.  These garments were made from the intestines of a seal, sealion, or bear.  The intestine is cut length wise and sewn together with a special stitch that would allow water to pass through. Beach grass was put into each seam so the stick wouldn’t pull through the material when the seam was tightened.  The grass would then swell up if water somehow got through…. further tightening the stitch keeping the water out.
When a young person got their first kill, they weren’t allowed to keep it. They had to give every piece of the animal away.  This wasn’t just to demonstrate their potential as a hunter.  It was meant to also teach them no one survives on their own and the responsibility of taking care of the elders and to not think of only themselves but to think of the needs of other – in other words empathy and generosity.

title: Agayutegpet, lla'apet
audio_transcript:
The word for sky in our Alutiiq language is “lla”.  If you say “llam” it means “of the sky”.  When you connect ‘llam” with “Sua”.  It means the spirit of the sky.  To live with the sky spirit - after your time on earth was done – required you live a proper life.  How is that accomplished?  All the answers are given to you in the stories passed from generation to generation. Humility – you are not the center of the universe.  You cannot survive without the help of others. Showing respect for you Elders and Ancestors.  Honoring the sacrifice of the animals.
A ceremony celebrated at the end of fall after hunting was completed was called the bladder festival. Nakaciuq.  It was believed when the hunter killed the animal the Sua “spirit” continued.  Until the animal is reborn the spirit resides in the bladder.  The bladders are removed from the animal and are inflated with air like a ballon.  They are hung from the ceiling during the celebration. When the ceremony is complete several days later the bladders are taken to the sea by the hunters and popped, releasing the spirits to be reborn again.  Sometime the hunter would send a message with the spirit.  They would say, remember how I treated you in life and death.  Tell your friends and bring them back with you next time. 
Wealth means different things to various cultures.  To some lots of money means wealth.  To our ancestors’ sharing food was a true sign of prosperity.  In some instances, a leader of a village might give away everything they own believing that “The more you give, the more you receive.”  Reciprocation wasn’t expected from the people gifts were given to.  The creator, “Llamsua” would make sure things would be repaid someday in the future.

title: Atkut
description: Alutiiq men wore hats woven from spruce root or crafted from wood. Similar to Lingít hats from Southeast Alaska, these garments were decorated with shells and beads, painted with bright colors, and considered a sign of wealth.

title: The Alutiiq Qayaq
description: The Alutiiq qayaq (kayak) represents one of the most sophisticated watercraft designs ever developed. Built with a driftwood or spruce frame and covered with sea lion skin, these sleek vessels were essential for hunting sea mammals, fishing, and traveling between islands. The qayaq's design—narrow, lightweight, and extremely maneuverable—allowed hunters to silently approach their prey and navigate the often treacherous waters around Kodiak Island. Paddlers developed remarkable skills, able to roll their kayaks upright if capsized and hunt in conditions that would be impossible in larger boats. This intimate relationship between the Alutiiq people and the ocean, embodied in the qayaq, sustained communities for thousands of years and remains a proud symbol of Alutiiq maritime heritage today.

title: Traditional Paddles
description: Handcrafted traditional Alutiiq paddles made by Jerry Laktonen
short_description: Monet's dreamy meditation on his beloved water garden

title: Ciqlluami
description: The traditional house - ciqlluami - was a wood framed structure covered in grass and sod.
audio_transcript:
Some may have heard the saying, “It takes a village to raise a child”. Involving extended family, neighbors, and community members helps contribute to the well-being of the children.  In Alutiiq tradition it’s the uncles and aunts that play a major role in the life lessons their nieces and nephews -needed- to survive.  Not learning these lessons could lead to injury of even death.  Your mother and father’s brothers and sisters could be sterner with the kids.  This could produce resentment towards them at first for their harshness but later in life when these life lessons are put into practice and they gain an awareness of why their uncles and aunts treated them in this way they hold the uncles and aunts in high esteem. 
In the winter when the family spends more time inside the ciqlluaq (the sod house) grandparents could take this opportunity to tell stories.  Of course, these were stories embedded with morals and traditions.  If a child violated the morals and traditions of their family, it would usually end with a punishment of some kind and a sit-down storytelling from a grandparent or elder.  If you violated the same morals and traditions again, you’d get the exact same story.  Obviously, you weren’t listening the first time.
Stories never had a moral at the end.  They would just - end.  It was up to the listener to decide what the story meant.  If the grandparents told you the moral, then the story would only have one meaning.  When there is no moral to the story the story evolves over time.  First, you listen to the story.  You grow up and you discover the story has multiple meanings.  You remember that story.  Then when you start a family of your own it’s your turn to teach them.
This was just one activity additional to all the activities described in this exhibit.

title: Asircarsuutet
description: Often referred to as the 'Mona Lisa of the North', this intimate portrait captures a young woman turning towards the viewer with an enigmatic expression. The luminous pearl earring and the stunning use of light on her face exemplify Vermeer's mastery of the medium.
short_description: Carving was a daily activity in Alutiiq communities. From hewing timbers to whittling lengths of bone and antler.
audio_transcript:
The discovery of ancient Alutiiq stone tools in Washington state has been a significant archeological find that sheds light on the early Native American history of the region.  These tools date back to a time when parts of the Pacific Northwest were covered in ice sheets.
What sets these tools apart from common Pacific Northwest artifacts is their design and craftsmanship—specifically the flaking pattern, grip angles, and composition, which closely align with Alutiiq artifacts found in Kodiak Island dig sites.
The discovery has sparked vigorous academic debate. While the Alutiiq people are primarily linked to southern coastal Alaska, marine travel along the Pacific was not uncommon in prehistoric times. Navigating by kayak could have enabled long-distance journeys for trade, seasonal hunting, or even settlement expansion.

Falling trees and splitting wood is a more recent development in the scope of time on Afognak and Northern Kodiak Island.  Our early ancestors had to collect driftwood from the beaches for building the frames of sod homes and the construction of tools.  The spruce tree has only taken root for the last 800 years on the Kodiak archipelago.  Before this time the island was wind swept tundra and grasslands.

title: Cimigtaanisqat
description: One of the most recognized paintings in Western art, this masterpiece depicts the view from Van Gogh's asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence at night. The swirling sky filled with energetic brushstrokes creates a dreamlike, almost turbulent atmosphere that contrasts with the peaceful village below.
short_description: A swirling, dreamlike nightscape that captures Van Gogh's emotional vision
audio_transcript:
Elders often say, "We are always getting ready."  In the summer people are getting ready for Winter.  In Winter people are getting ready for Summer.  If you aren't prepared for the return of the salmon when they arrive what chance does your family have to catch enough fish for the winter.  Are your fish drying racks clean and ready?  Is your fishing equipment ready for use?  These are questions that need to be answered before the fish arrive.
Always be prepared for an opportunity.  You may not get a second chance.  My dad told me a story about how he would take a shotgun to school.  He would leave his gun outside the door of the classroom.  If a duck happens to present itself on the way to school or home the duck would help provide for the family.
Certain land animals mentioned on the panels in this exhibit aren't indigenous to Kodiak or Afognak Islands:  Black tailed Deer, elk, mountain goat, beaver, snowshoe hare, reindeer, were introduced between 1920 and 1950.  The only mammals Native to Kodiak are the red fox, river otter, ermine, tundra vole, little brown bat, and the Kodiak bear.
The items in the display are tools used to hunt and fish for our food. All our materials came from the natural environment.  Stone, wood, grass, animal bone and skins.
Today we use modern materials and tools to collect our resources we need to survive.  We also supplement our diets with store bought food but the reason we do this is the same.  To provide for our families.  Like the seasons these are "Things that Never Change."
